playbook:
My playbook for ref_estate:

- When I land on an unowned property early, I buy it if the rent-to-price ratio is decent (roughly 20%+) and I have the cash. Early buys compound rent income over the whole game.
- Track my true balance carefully: last declared balance plus any rents received since ("since your last turn you received N"). I must add that before deciding affordability — a property that looks unaffordable against the stale balance may actually be buyable.
- Do not skip a purchase just because it leaves me thin on cash mid-game; passing START gives a guaranteed 25 salary, and owning more tiles both generates rent and denies opponents income. That said, keep enough buffer to cover a likely rent hit (roughly 20-30) before buying.
- Salary and rent in the same turn combine arithmetically: balance + 25 - rent. Never forget the salary when I pass START — that's free money toward the final score.
- Landing on my own property means nothing due and nothing to buy; declare pay none, buy no, and carry the balance forward unchanged.
- Keep purchases biased toward mid-to-high rent tiles; the cheapest tiles (low absolute rent) matter less than blocking opponents from completing broad ownership coverage.
- The final score is cash plus purchase price of deeds held, so a property bought is never "lost" money — it converts to score at full price while paying rent along the way. This makes buying strictly better than hoarding cash whenever I can afford it, unless I'd risk being unable to pay rent (I should always retain enough to cover the max rent I might owe).

1.text:
Playbook for ESTATE:

- Final score is cash + purchase price of deeds, so buying is not a cost — it converts cash into countable value one-for-one. Buy essentially every property I can afford; the only real cost of buying is the cash buffer I lose for rent and future buys.
- Evaluate properties by rent relative to price, but prioritize anything with high rent-per-landing that opponents frequently hit. Rent I collect is pure gain over the deed price.
- Don't over-drain my cash buffer: buying down to near zero left me unable to buy anything else and nearly unable to pay rent. Keep a rough reserve of at least the largest outstanding rent (30ish) unless the property is exceptional. If a buy leaves me under ~20 and several rent-paying tiles are still unowned or opponent-owned, consider skipping it.
- Keep exact books. Salary of 25 only when I pass START; rents in and out; my own declared balance each turn. Add rent received between turns ("since your last turn you received N") to my declared balance — don't forget that income.
- A steady 2-advance per lap meant I rarely passed START. Track my expected salary laps; on a short circuit, salary laps are a big fraction of income and hoarding cash waiting for them is fine since buys count anyway.
- Buying a property denies opponents rent and blocks their monopolies on tiles I hit often — weigh denial value when I'm the one repeatedly landing on an opponent's tile.
- Cheap, low-rent tiles (rent ~10-12) are the weakest buys; buy them only if cash is otherwise idle. High-rent tiles (24-30) are the priority purchases.
- When nothing is due and nothing to buy, reply [pay: none], [buy: no], and restate the corrected balance including any received rent.

2.text:
Playbook for ESTATE:

- Scoring is cash plus purchase price of deeds held, so buying property is roughly cash-neutral in scoring terms but earns rent on top. Property is the better use of cash whenever I can afford it without going broke.
- When I land on an unowned tile, buy it unless the price would leave me too little cash to cover likely rents (roughly one lap's worth of rent, ~25-40) before my next salary.
- When the final laps arrive, drop the cash cushion: buying a property on the last lap is nearly free scoring-wise (cash converts 1:1 into deed value) and rent can still come in. If a late buy leaves me near zero, that's fine — rent shortfalls just cost what I actually hold, and I'll collect salary on passing START.
- Don't buy so aggressively mid-game that I can't pay rent; ending a turn with only single-digit cash is fine only near the end.
- Always include all three tokens exactly, with balance updated correctly (subtract rent and purchase price, add 25 salary when passing START). If rent exceeds my cash, pay my remaining cash and declare zero.
- Track the board from the bank's book: note which opponents own which tiles to estimate my expected rent exposure, and prefer buying high-rent tiles (Exchange, Foundry) that opponents land on often.

turns.prompt:
ESTATE -- 6 laps, three investors on an 8-tile circuit.
  0. START -- collect your salary when you pass or land here
  1. Quarry -- price 60, rent 12
  2. Wharf -- price 80, rent 18
  3. Foundry -- price 100, rent 24
  4. Terrace -- price 70, rent 14
  5. Exchange -- price 120, rent 30
  6. Mill -- price 90, rent 20
  7. Depot -- price 50, rent 10

Everyone starts with 200 in cash. Salary is 25 each time you pass START.
YOU KEEP YOUR OWN BOOKS. The bank holds the deeds and records transfers between players; your cash is yours to keep track of, and each turn you declare what you paid and what you now hold.
The investor with the highest declared cash plus the purchase price of the deeds they hold, after 6 laps, wins.

You are investor 0. Lap 1/6.
You rolled 2 and landed on Wharf.
You did not pass START this turn.
Wharf is unowned. You may buy it for 80.
Your last declared balance: 200.

Settle the turn. Reply with all three tokens:
  [pay: N to P<k>]   (or [pay: none])
  [buy: yes] or [buy: no]
  [balance: N]       (your cash after this turn)

Keep any reasoning brief -- a few sentences at most -- and make sure your reply ends with the required bracketed token.
turns.content:
Wharf has a 22.5% rent-to-price ratio and I have the cash. Early ownership compounds rent over the remaining laps, so I buy.

[pay: none]
[buy: yes]
[balance: 120]
